sentences.text: The defining feature of this genus is a single, elongated tooth roughly one centimetre in length.
Edward Drinker Cope initially misidentified the holotype as belonging to a plesiosaur before correcting his assessment within the same year.
The species Paronychodon caperatus is known from the Hell Creek Formation of North Dakota, Montana, and South Dakota, as well as the Lance Formation of Wyoming.
A second species, Paronychodon caperatus, is based on holotype YPM 10624, a tooth similar in form to P. lacustris but somewhat larger.
Paronychodon has been classified variously as a coelurid, ornithomimosaur, dromaeosaurid, archaeopterygid, or troodontid, though it may be another type of coelurosaurian theropod.
The family classification for Paronychodon is tentatively listed as Troodontidae.
Paronychodon lived at the end of the Cretaceous period, 70 million years ago, during the Maastrichtian in North America.
While most researchers consider Paronychodon to represent indeterminate theropod teeth, a small consensus suggests the teeth belong to Deinonychosauria.
No jaws from adult individuals bearing identical Paronychodon teeth have ever been found.
Othniel Charles Marsh suggested that Paronychodon teeth were pathological, formed when lower jaw teeth accidentally grew back-to-back on the mandible suture.
Many specimens referred to Paronychodon include varied teeth such as serrated ones, low ones, and those without a flattened side.
